newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-EUROPEAN STOCKS RECOVER ON UPBEAT GREENSPAN.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EUROPEAN STOCKS RECOVER ON UPBEAT GREENSPAN.

text.p: European stocks shook off early
jitters on Tuesday after Federal Reserve chairman Alan
Greenspan gave a positive report on the U.S. economy and failed
to deliver the warning on overheating markets many investors
had feared.
Share markets, seeking an excuse to correct after a bull
run, fell in the morning as dealers worried that Greenspan
might hint at higher interest rates when he testified to the
Senate.
Anxiety was only to be expected. Greenspan wiped billions
of dollars off share values worldwide when he said last
December that financial markets had become irrationally
exuberant.
Since then the Dow Jones Industrial Average has risen about
400 points. But in his statement to the Senate budget
committee, he described the stock market performance only as
breathtaking.
Greenspan warned about the dangers of wage-driven inflation
but was otherwise upbeat. "The economy has retained
considerable vigour, with few signs of the imbalances and
inflationary tensions that have disrupted past expansions," he
said.
The Dow dipped as Greenspan spoke but investors could not
resist the temptation to buy on the dips and by 1710 GMT it was
was up 24.63 points from Monday's record close at 6,868.50.
European markets, which had a rocky ride before the Senate
testimony, took heart from Greenspan.
London's FTSE-100, spooked in the morning by an interest
rate warning from the British central bank governor, recovered
from early losses to close up 1.5 points at 4,195.5.
"He's not said anything the market didn't expect," said
Gerard Lyons, economist at DKB International. "He gave no signs
of an imminent rate hike but he will remain vigilant to
inflationary pressures."
Greenspan helped wipe out a bout of nerves triggered by his
British counterpart, Eddie George, who continued his campaign
for higher interest rates with a warning that there were real
dangers in letting sterling strength delay a rate rise.
German shares also gained heart from Greenspan after
morning falls triggered by an index from the IFO organisation
indicating that the business climate remained soft.
The DAX index, which fell through the 3,000 point barrier
in early trade, closed down 53.97 points at 2,976.71. But the
Greenspan factor emerged in after-hours electronic trading,
with the IBIS DAX-30 index closing back at 3,000.66, up 1.47.
Paris followed the roller coaster trend, with the CAC-40
index well down in the morning but closing post-Greenspan at
"Greenspan reassured the markets with his comments. Wall
Street went up and so did we," one trader said. "But you have
to be careful when you remember the impact he had last time."
The dollar took a breather after hitting an almost four
year high against the yen on Monday. It closed little changed
in Europe, underpinned by Greenspan but unable to build on
gains made after his speech.
"A lot of excitement had been built into Greenspan's
comments before they were made. What he actually said was very
much on the lines of what a prudent central banker would say,"
said Teis Knuthsen, international economist at First Chicago.
The dollar was steady in late European trading at 1.6240
marks compared with Monday's late European level of 1.6258.
Against the yen it eased to 117.78 after breaching the 118
barrier for the first time in almost four years on Monday.
